title: DEEPAK RAHEJA VS. OMKARA ASSETS RECONSTRUCTION PRIVATE LTD.

paras.text:
2026 INSC 1134
 C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 1 of 50
REPORTABLE
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.12195 OF 2025
DEEPAK RAHEJA AND
ANOTHER ... APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
OMKARA ASSETS
RECONSTRUCTION PRIVATE
LTD. AND ANOTHER ... RESPONDENT(S)
WITH
CIVIL APPEAL NO. OF 2026
(ARISING OUT OF DIARY NO.58001 OF 2025)
J U D G M E N T
AUGUSTINE GEORGE MASIH, J.
1. These two statutory appeals under Section 62 of the
Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (hereinafter,
"the Code") assail the common judgment dated
19.08.2025 of the National Company Law Appellate
Tribunal, Principal Bench, New Delhi (hereinafter,

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 2 of 50
"the Appellate Tribunal") in Company Appeal (AT)
(Insolvency) No. 1040 of 2025 and the connected
Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1039 of 2025,
dismissing both appeals and affirming two orders of
even date, 08.07.2025, of the National Company Law
Tribunal, Mumbai Bench, Court-I (hereinafter, "the
Adjudicating Authority"), which admitted Company
Petition (IB) No. 291 of 2023 and Company Petition
(IB) No. 290 of 2023 under Section 7 of the Code and
initiating the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process
(hereinafter, "CIRP") against GSTAAD Hotels Pvt. Ltd.
and Neo Capricorn Plaza Pvt. Ltd. respectively.
2. The facts, issues, submissions and material in both
appeals being substantially common, it is convenient
to dispose them by a common judgment, setting out
the facts as they arise in Civil Appeal No. 12195 of
2025, pertaining to GSTAAD Hotels Pvt. Ltd.
(hereinafter, "the Corporate Debtor"), with reference to
the connected appeal pertaining to Neo Capricorn
Plaza Pvt. Ltd. (hereinafter, "Neo") as and when
necessary. The Appellate Tribunal adopted the same
course, and no party suggests that any material
distinction arises.
3. By a Loan Agreement dated 26.12.2017 (hereinafter,
"the Loan Agreement"), Piramal Finance Ltd., as it was

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 3 of 50
then known (subsequently Piramal Capital and
Housing Finance Ltd., hereinafter "PCHFL"), extended
a term loan facility aggregating Rs.600 crores to the
Corporate Debtor and Neo as co-borrowers: a term
loan of Rs.450 crores and a Rolling Credit Facility
(hereinafter "RCF") of Rs.50 crores to the Corporate
Debtor, and a term loan of Rs.100 crores to Neo. The
Corporate Debtor owns and operates the JW Marriott
Hotel at Bangalore; Neo owns and operates the
Crowne Plaza Hotel at Pune.
4. A Cash Management Agreement (hereinafter "the
CMA") was executed in January 2018 between the
Lender, the Corporate Debtor and the Hotel Operator
i.e. Marriott Hotels India Private Limited, under which
the gross revenue collections of the hotels were to be
deposited into a Revenue Account, of which 66 per
cent was to be transferred daily into an Expense
Account for the operating expenses of the hotels, and
34 per cent into a Retention Account towards
servicing of the debt.
5. The Loan Agreement further obliged the maintenance
of a Debt Service Reserve Account (hereinafter "the
DSRA") of Rs.8 crores for the Corporate debtor's
facilities, under Clause 9 read with the Eleventh
Schedule, to be appropriated towards interest and

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 4 of 50
principal shortfalls, a DSRA of Rs.2 crores being
contemplated for Neo. It is undisputed that Rs.3
crores of that reserve remained undisbursed as on
15.11.2022.
6. The Corporate Debtor additionally availed two
facilities under the Government of India's Emergency
Credit Line Guarantee Scheme (hereinafter "ECLGS"):
ECLGS Facility-1 of Rs.98 crores sanctioned on
29.12.2020 and ECLGS Facility-2 of Rs.65 crores
sanctioned on 11.03.2022, each under a separate
agreement. A connected ECLGS facility of Rs.19.5
crores was sanctioned to Neo by an agreement dated
30.12.2020.
7. Clauses 27.1 and 27.2 of the Loan Agreement dated
26.12.2017 vested in the lenders an absolute right of
assignment, exercisable unilaterally and without the
borrower's consent. On 27.12.2022, PCHFL and PHL
Fininvest Pvt. Ltd. (subsequently Piramal Enterprises
Ltd., hereinafter "PEL") in accordance with these
clauses 27.1 and 27.2 of the loan agreement, executed
an Assignment Agreement in favour of Omkara Asset
Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. (hereinafter "Omkara" or "the
Financial Creditor"), assigning the Term Loan, the
RCF, ECLGS-1 and ECLGS-2 in respect of both
companies.

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 5 of 50
8. On 09.02.2023, four separate Form-D filings
recording defaults by the corporate debtor and Neo
were registered with National E-Governance Services
Ltd. (hereinafter "NeSL"), the Information Utility with
which the facilities stood registered, in respect of the
Term Loan, the RCF, ECLGS-1 and ECLGS-2
respectively.
9. On 15.02.2023, Omkara recalled the entire
outstanding under all four facilities, calling upon the
Corporate Debtor to pay Rs.666,53,26,968/- within
three days, and upon Neo, by a separate notice,
Rs.119,99,23,320/-. The notice of recall recorded that
failure to pay any instalment and coupon constitutes
an event of default entitling the lenders and the
security trustee to exercise all their rights under the
Loan Agreement and the ECLGS Loan Agreements.
10. On 09.03.2023, Omkara filed CP (IB) No. 291 of 2023
against the Corporate Debtor and CP (IB) No. 290 of
2023 against Neo under Section 7 of the Code. The
date of default in respect of the Loan, ECLGS Facility-1 and ECLGS Facility-2 was stated to be 15.11.2022,
the total amount claimed in default being
Rs.665,74,77,237/- as on 27.02.2023. By two
separate orders dated 09.01.2024 the Adjudicating
Authority admitted both petitions, initiated CIRP,

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 6 of 50
declared a moratorium under Section 14 of the Code
and appointed an Interim Resolution Professional.
11. Meanwhile, the Corporate Debtor on 10th March,
2023 filed Writ Petition No. 6037 of 2023 before the
High Court of Karnataka impugning the Assignment
Agreement dated 27.12.2022 as contrary to the
Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets
and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002 and
the circulars of the Reserve Bank of India, on the
ground that its account had never been classified as
a non-performing asset or a special mention account.
The learned Single Judge, High Court of Karnataka,
dismissed Writ Petition No. 6037 of 2023 on
28.02.2024, upholding the Assignment Agreement.
The Division Bench dismissed Writ Appeal No. 478 of
2024 on 19.05.2024 against the order dated
28.02.2024 and the Special Leave Petition against the
writ appeal order dated 19.05.2024 was dismissed by
this Court on 25.08.2025. In these parallel
proceedings, instituted by the Corporate Debtor itself,
both the Single Judge and the Division Bench
recorded its submission that it had not contested that
the principal or interest payment was overdue at any
point of time, the High Court further holding that the
corporate debtor's accounts were irregular.

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 7 of 50
12. The orders dated 09.01.2024 of the Adjudicating
authority admitting the Section 7 applications were
challenged in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos.
165 and 212 of 2024. By an interim order dated
24.01.2024 the Appellate Tribunal directed that the
Committee of Creditors may not be constituted
meanwhile, while requiring that no hindrance be
caused to the running of the hotels. By a common
judgment dated 08.01.2025 it framed eleven issues,
allowed both appeals, set aside the admission orders
and revived both company petitions to be heard
afresh, its operative direction being in these terms:
"65. We make it clear that while deciding these
Appeal(s), we are not expressing any conclusive
opinion on any of the issues, which are yet to be
decided by the Adjudicating Authority consequent
to this remand order. Parties shall bear their own
costs."
13. In so remanding, the Appellate Tribunal indicated the
questions requiring fresh consideration. These
questions, inter-alia were that the CMA ought not to
have been disregarded merely because its existence
had been denied by the Financial Creditor; that the
amounts transferred under it towards servicing of
debt required consideration before any finding of
default; that the DSRA had not been adverted to at all;
that the question whether there had been any

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 8 of 50
admission of default required consideration; and that
the submission concerning utilisation of the ECLGS
proceeds to service the lenders' own dues had been
rejected upon an end-use certificate alone. Upon each
of these matters the Appellate Tribunal expressly
disclaimed any conclusive opinion.
14. Pursuant to the remand both the parties filed
additional affidavits, replies and sur-rejoinders and
were heard at length by the Adjudicating Authority.
The Corporate Debtor placed upon record two Review
Reports of BK Ramadhyani & Co. LLP, Chartered
Accountants, questioning the rate of interest applied
by the erstwhile lenders and the treatment of the
DSRA and ECLGS amounts. It is of some significance,
and is recorded in the order of the Adjudicating
Authority, that that review did not find any fault in
the computation of the default amount, but
questioned the quantum only upon the ground of the
alleged inappropriateness of the rate of interest
applied. The distinction is material and will be
adverted to below.
15. After hearing both parties afresh, the Adjudicating
Authority by its order dated 08.07.2025 again
admitted both petitions, recording a finding that there
exists a financial debt exceeding the threshold

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 9 of 50
prescribed under Section 4 of the Code and that the
same is in default, that the petition was complete in
all respects and it accordingly deserved to be
admitted.
16. The Appellate Tribunal upon challenge affirmed each
of the findings in the Adjudicating Authority's order
dated 08.07.2025. These findings of the two forums,
for the sake of brevity are recorded together.
17. Upon the CMA, it was held that Clause 18.39 of that
agreement makes it emphatically clear that the CMA
and the Escrow Arrangement put in place only a
mechanism to channel an agreed percentage of
revenue towards debt servicing, and do not constitute
an exhaustive arrangement discharging the
underlying obligation to repay from any other source
acceptable to the Lender, the Appellate Tribunal
adding that the balance in the Retention Account
nonetheless remains relevant to whether sufficient
funds were available. Upon the alleged excess
withdrawal of Rs.10,35,88,444/- beyond the 34 per
cent ratio, it was held that under Clause 1.B(iv)(a) of
the CMA the obligation to deposit any overdrawn
amount is cast upon both the Financier and the
Owner and that the overdrawn amounts had in any
event been appropriated towards obligations the

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 10 of 50
Corporate Debtor was bound to discharge under
Clause 18.39 of the CMA. It was further held that the
overdrawn amounts related to the period of April and
May 2023 and not to November 2022 to February
2023 period which is relevant to the application and
a refund referable to a period of April-May 2023 would
only have increased the default amount. The Clause 2
of the CMA vested with the Operator a right to
terminate the Operating Agreement but the Operator
never exercised this right and that it was not the
Corporate Debtor's case that the amount withdrawn
exceeded the Lenders' entitlement.
18. Upon the computation of default as on 15.11.2022,
the Adjudicating Authority examined the Statement of
Accounts for 15.11.2022 to 30.04.2024, furnished by
the Financial Creditor and produced before it by the
Corporate Debtor itself. It found interest outstanding
under ECLGS-I and ECLGS-II of Rs.1,38,64,767/-
and Rs.1,14,59,589/-, and two instalments
aggregating Rs.4,08,33,334/- unpaid under ECLGS-I, the total default under the two facilities being
Rs.5,46,98,101/- and Rs.1,14,59,589/-. That Clause
17.39 of the ECLGS Agreements was identical to
Clause 18.39 of the CMA and although
Rs.1,54,93,481.68/- lying in the Retention Account

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 11 of 50
was appropriated on 24.11.2022 towards the Loan
and RCF accounts, the ECLGS dues remained in
default even thereafter.
19. Upon the DSRA, testing the contention upon the
Corporate Debtor's own methodology, the
Adjudicating Authority found that interest
outstanding across all facilities aggregated to
Rs.9,87,30,348/-, besides default interest of
Rs.2,90,87,114/-. That Clause 29.1 of the loan
agreement requires part payments to be appropriated
pro-rata, first towards default interest, subsequently
towards interest and then towards the principal
amount. That neither ECLGS Agreement contains any
DSRA provision, nor extends to those facilities the
DSRA created under the Loan Agreement. It was
observed that even assuming the appropriation of the
undisbursed Rs.3 crores under the DSRA and leaving
the default interest component wholly out of account
then also only Rs.75,95,006/- could be applied
toward the ECLGS interest, leaving a default of
Rs.1,76,29,350/- in interest besides the default of
principal amount of Rs.4,08,33,334/-. The Appellate
Tribunal recorded that no liability arose upon the
undisbursed sum under the DSRA, that its
disbursement could itself have carried interest, and

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 12 of 50
that the finding of a subsisting default could not be
faulted.
20. Upon the right of recall, it was held that, the first
disbursement having taken place on 28.12.2017 and
five years having expired on 27.12.2022, the right to
recall accrued dehors any default under Clause 7.2.6
of the loan agreement, to which the recall notice
referred. Upon solvency, it was concluded, after
examining revenue, operating expenses, the owner's
profit and the liabilities, that the material belied the
claim of solvency founded merely upon a positive
EBITDA, the Corporate Debtor having failed to service
its interest and principal obligations month upon
month until December 2023, and that no exceptional
circumstance warranted the exercise of discretion,
assuming any to exist under Section 7.
21. Upon res judicata, the Appellate Tribunal held that
paragraph 65 of its remand judgment made clear that
no conclusive opinion had been expressed upon any
issue left for decision, the observations there going
only to the unsustainability of the earlier conclusions
for non-consideration of relevant material. Upon the
One-Time Settlement, it held that the revised proposal
of Rs.743.71 crores, brought on record by the
Appellant himself, made it clear that debt and default

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 13 of 50
stood admitted. Upon the authorities, it held that the
proposition that an event of default must arise from
the agreement admitted of no dispute, that event
being noticed in Clause 19 of the loan agreement. It
concluded that no ground existed to interfere with the
orders dated 08.07.2025 of the Adjudicating
Authority.
22. Learned senior counsel for the Appellants, while
assailing the aforesaid findings firstly contends that
the findings recorded in the remand order,
particularly upon the CMA, the DSRA and the alleged
diversion of the ECLGS proceeds attained finality and
operated as res judicata. That the CMA, if properly
applied, would show that debt-servicing obligations
were in fact being met through the Retention Account,
and that the excess withdrawal of Rs.10,35,88,444/-
from the retention account would establish that there
was no default upon 15.11.2022 in the loan account
or under the ECLGS facilities. The Section 7
application pleaded no facts of default in the Term
Loan account, the default being confined to the
ECLGS facilities, which were not even due and
payable on that date.
23. It was further contended that the DSRA of Rs.8 crores
for the Corporate Debtor's facilities and Rs.2 crores

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 14 of 50
for Neo existed solely for appropriation against a
default in the Term Loan payments, the ECLGS
facilities and any interest thereon, and that its
utilisation would have ensured that no default
occurred in the first place. On the Corporate debtor's
and Neo's financial position, it was submitted that
they both are profit-earning companies, successfully
running the two hotels, with positive EBITDA of Rs.81
crores and Rs.10 crores respectively in the financial
year 2022-23 and the impugned order has put two
running hotels into insolvency, which is not the
purpose and object of the Code. Lastly, reliance was
placed upon Vidarbha Industries Power Ltd. v. Axis
Bank Ltd.1 for the propositions that an event of default
must arise from the agreement between the parties,
that any discretion available to the Adjudicating
Authority is not to be exercised arbitrarily or
capriciously, and that the cash liquidity and financial
health of the corporate debtor are relevant
considerations.
24. Per contra, learned senior counsel for Respondent
No.1 submits that Omkara's status as an assignee
and consequently as a financial creditor under
Section 5(7) of the Code stands conclusively
1 (2022) 8 SCC 352

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 15 of 50
established by the Assignment Agreement read with
Clauses 27.1 and 27.2 of the loan agreement which
was infact independently upheld by the High Court of
Karnataka as well as by this Court. That the Appellate
Tribunal having expressly refrained from any
conclusive opinion, the fresh consideration it directed
was in fact undertaken and the Corporate Debtor
never denied the existence of a debt, its entire defence
proceeding upon the footing that default could be
cured through appropriation of the DSRA and the
CMA amounts, which is in substance a concession
that default did occur, the only live dispute being one
of quantum and curability rather than existence.
25. It was further submitted that the total default as on
15.11.2022 was Rs.17,16,29,518/- in respect of the
Corporate Debtor and a minimum of
Rs.2,64,99,473/- in respect of Neo. The CMA, the
learned senior counsel contended, was no more than
a mechanism for the cash flow operations of the
hotels. The insufficiency in the Retention Account
meant that the borrowers were bound to pay from
other funds acceptable to the Lender and that any
amount withdrawn was appropriated towards the
debt obligation of the debtors, it not being the
Appellants' case that any sum exceeding the

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 16 of 50
obligation was withdrawn. The DSRA amount lay
within the total sanctioned loan quantum and its
disbursement would have increased both the loan and
the interest liability. Reliance was placed upon
Innoventive Industries Ltd. v. ICICI Bank2, E.S.
Krishnamurthy v. Bharath Hi-Tech Builders (P) Ltd.
3,
M. Suresh Kumar Reddy v. Canara Bank,
4 the review
order in Axis Bank Ltd. v. Vidarbha Industries Power
Ltd.5, Maitreya Doshi v. Anand Rathi Global Finance
Ltd.,
6 Devas Multimedia (P) Ltd. v. Antrix Corpn. Ltd.7,
and Kalyani Transco v. Bhushan Power & Steel Ltd8.
26. We have heard learned senior counsel for the parties
at length and have perused the record.
27. At the outset it would be apposite to advert to the
scope of appeal under Section 62(1) of the Code.
Section 62(1) permits an appeal to this Court against
an order of the Appellate Tribunal "on a question of
law arising out of such order". This Court is not
required or obliged, as a first appellate court might be,
to undertake a fresh appraisal of evidence or to
reassess concurrent findings of fact. Where the
2 (2018) 1 SCC 407
3 (2022) 3 SCC 161
4 (2023) 8 SCC 387
5 (2023) 7 SCC 321
6 (2023) 17 SCC 606
7 (2023) 1 SCC 216
8 2025 SCC OnLine SC 2093

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 17 of 50
findings upon the existence of a financial debt, the
occurrence of default, the authenticity of documents
or the acknowledgment of liability are recorded by the
Adjudicating Authority, these on being affirmed by the
Appellate Tribunal, attain the character of concurrent
findings of fact, and therefore, any interference is
warranted only where they are shown to be perverse,
based upon no evidence, arrived at by ignoring
material evidence, or founded upon an erroneous
legal standard. The expression "on a question of law"
excludes a re-hearing upon facts. An appellant
cannot, under the guise of raising a question of law,
invite this Court to re-weigh evidence or substitute its
own conclusions for those concurrently arrived at
findings by the tribunals below.
28. That restraint is not merely a matter of statutory
construction. The Adjudicating Authority and the
Appellate Tribunal are specialised tribunals,
constituted with a combination of judicial and
technical members, precisely so that matters
requiring close engagement with accounts, ledgers,
financial covenants and commercial documents may
be resolved by bodies possessed of the relevant
expertise. The Bankruptcy Law Reforms Committee
(BLRC), as noticed by this Court in Swiss Ribbons Pvt.

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 18 of 50
Ltd. v. Union of India9, had identified as a defect of the
antecedent regime that the fora entrusted with
insolvency may lack the business or financial
expertise, information or bandwidth to decide such
matters and the constitution of specialised tribunals
was the legislative answer. Where two such bodies
have concurrently examined the same statements of
account, the same CMA and DSRA clauses and the
same Review Reports, and arrived at the same finding
of default upon the same date, this Court ought not
lightly to substitute its own reading of that material
for theirs. That principle, articulated in Maitreya
Doshi (supra) and Devas Multimedia (supra), applies
with particular force under the Code. In Kalyani
Transco (supra) it was held that where a concurrent
view has been taken by two adjudicating authorities
under a special statute, interference is unwarranted
unless that view was in ignorance of mandatory
statutory provisions, based upon extraneous
consideration, or ex-facie arbitrary or illegal.
29. It follows that the question before this Court is not
whether the arithmetic of the Adjudicating Authority
could have been undertaken differently, or whether
some alternative appropriation methodology might
9 (2019) 4 SCC 17

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 19 of 50
have yielded a different figure. The question is
whether the two forums applied the correct legal
standard in determining that a default within the
meaning of the Code had occurred. That is a question
of law, and it is that question which this Court
proceeds to answer, after first clearing away the
threshold objection.
30. The threshold objection is that Omkara is not a
financial creditor within the meaning of Section 5(7)
of the Code at all, so that the condition precedent for
an application under Section 7 is wanting. Section
5(7) defines a financial creditor as any person to
whom a financial debt is owed and expressly "includes
a person to whom such debt has been legally assigned
or transferred to". The scope of the definition is
unequivocal, and the only question is whether the
assignment in favour of Omkara was a legal
assignment. That question has been litigated to
finality, upto this Court, when the SLP challenging the
Division Bench judgement of the Karnataka High
Court was dismissed on 25.08.2025. The legality,
validity and enforceability of the assignment was
directly and substantially in issue in those
proceedings, and the determination stands
conclusively settled inter partes.

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 20 of 50
31. The attempt to reopen the validity of that assignment
of debt is barred by the principles underlying issue
estoppel. Issue estoppel arises where a particular
issue, forming a necessary ingredient in a cause of
action, has been litigated and decided in a first action,
and, in subsequent proceedings between the same
parties involving a different cause of action to which
the same issue is relevant, one of the parties seeks to
reopen that issue. Three elements in that regard must
be satisfied i.e. identity of issue, finality of the earlier
decision upon the merits, and identity of parties or
their privies; each of which is satisfied here. The
doctrine rests upon finality, consistency and judicial
discipline, and once a finding has attained finality
between the parties, neither party may seek a fresh
adjudication upon the same issue merely because the
subsequent proceedings arise under a different
statute or seek a different relief. To permit the
Appellants to reopen a concluded legal issue in the
present proceedings would tantamount to a collateral
attack upon binding determinations that have
attained finality up to this Court.
32. There is a further and independent reason apart from
issue estoppel that bars the challenge to the validity
of the assignment agreement before the tribunals

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 21 of 50
below. The jurisdiction of the Adjudicating Authority
under Section 7 is confined to determining the
existence of a financial debt and the occurrence of
default. It is not an appellate forum over judgments
rendered by competent constitutional courts. The
status of the assignee having been conclusively
affirmed, the Adjudicating Authority could not have
undertaken a de novo examination of the validity of
assignment, and it did not err in declining to do so.
33. With the status of the Respondent no.1 as a financial
creditor established, and the existence of the
underlying financial debt itself being undisputed, the
appeals stand reduced to the questions of law now to
be framed.
34. The Accounting disputes aside, these appeals
principally concern the question of what a financial
creditor must establish to prove a default under
section 3(12) of the Code. Two questions of law arise
from the same:
QUESTION I: What is the evidentiary threshold
required to satisfy the Adjudicating Authority that a
"default" within the meaning of Sections 3(12) and 7
of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 has
occurred?

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 22 of 50
QUESTION II: What nature of documentary material
may legitimately be relied upon by the Adjudicating
Authority for recording a satisfaction that a "default"
within the meaning of Section 7 has occurred?
35. Before turning to the statutory scheme, it is pertinent
to recall the legislative purpose that underlines the
Code. The Code is, first and foremost, a legislation for
the time-bound reorganisation and resolution of
corporate debtors, so that the value of a stressed
enterprise is preserved rather than allowed to erode
through delay. Speed is not an incidental virtue of the
Code, it is its central design principle. The
architecture of Section 7, including the fourteen-day
period for ascertaining default under sub-section (4),
is built around the elimination of exactly the kind of
delay that was the characteristic of the antecedent
regime.
36. The means by which the Code secures that expedition
must next be noticed, for the legislature did not treat
every creditor alike in prescribing what must be
shown before the process is set in motion. The
distinction between financial and operational
creditors under the Code is instructive in this regard.
Financial contracts generally involve large sums and
specified repayment schedules, defaults entitling the

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 23 of 50
creditor to recall the loan in totality, whereas
operational contracts carry no such stipulation and
are recurring in nature. Financial debts owed to
banks and financial institutions are, by their very
nature, well-documented, and a default committed in
respect of them is readily verifiable. That
characteristic is the evidentiary premise upon which
the trigger mechanism for financial creditors rests,
and it explains why the Code dispenses, in their case,
with the notice-and-dispute machinery prescribed by
Sections 8 and 9 of the Code for operational creditors.
The same asymmetry is carried into the statutory
obligations of the two classes: Section 215(2) of the
Code requires that a financial creditor shall submit
financial information and information relating to
assets over which a security interest has been
created, whereas Section 215(3) of the Code provides
only that an operational creditor may do so.
37. The Bankruptcy Law Reforms Committee (BLRC)
report explained the rationale in terms leaving no
room for doubt. Since financial creditors have
electronic records of their liabilities filed with the
Information Utilities, an incontrovertible event of
default upon any financial credit contract is readily
verifiable by accessing that system, whereas the

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 24 of 50
evidence available to an operational creditor may be
electronic or physical and until such time as the
Information Utilities became ubiquitous, financial
creditors might establish default in a manner similar
to operational creditors. Two propositions of
importance emerge, first, that an Information Utility
record was conceived as the primary and readily
verifiable evidence of a financial creditor's default and
second, that other means of proof were expressly
contemplated in the meanwhile. The Code was thus
designed from the outset with a hierarchy of proof in
contemplation, an Information Utility record at the
apex and other documentary material in the
alternative.
38. The object of establishing Information Utilities was
that considerable time was previously lost before all
parties obtained the relevant information, that
disputes upon such facts could consume years in
court, and that it accordingly envisaged a competitive
industry of information utilities holding an array of
information about all firms at all times, so that upon
commencement of the resolution process undisputed
and complete information would become available to
all persons involved within less than a day. An
interpretation of Section 7 requiring the Adjudicating

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 25 of 50
Authority to reconcile every contested ledger entry
before recording its satisfaction would defeat that
purpose entirely, and would restore the very mischief
the Code was enacted to remedy.
39. In Innoventive Industries (supra), this Court had
explained the operational terms in which the scheme
of Section 7 would operate which applies fully to the
present enquiry. It held that the moment the
Adjudicating Authority is satisfied that a default has
occurred, the application must be admitted unless it
is incomplete. It further held that the Adjudicating
Authority has merely to see the records of the
information utility or other evidence produced by the
financial creditor to satisfy itself that a default has
occurred, and that it is of no matter that the debt is
disputed so long as the debt is due.
40. Against the backdrop of the legal position enunciated
above, the starting point to answer the first question
of law formulated by this Court must be the statutory
definition. Section 3(12) of the Code provides:
"(12) 'default' means non-payment of debt when
whole or any part or instalment of the amount of debt
has become due and payable and is not paid by the
debtor or the corporate debtor, as the case may be;"
41. The definition is deliberately undemanding. It neither
requires that the entire debt be due, nor that the full

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 26 of 50
quantum be free of dispute, but only that some part
of what is due and payable has not been paid. The
words "whole or any part or instalment" are not
inessential, they are the operative words of the
definition, and they establish that the statutory
conception of default is satisfied by a shortfall,
however partial.
42. It follows that a fundamental distinction must be
maintained between two matters which the
Appellants' submissions persistently conflate. The
occurrence of default is a historical and static event
which crystallises upon the date a debt became due
and was not paid. The quantum of debt outstanding,
by contrast, is dynamic, fluctuating upon account of
accruing interest, default interest, charges,
adjustments and part-repayments. The two enquiries
are different in kind, and Section 7 is concerned with
the first i.e. the occurrence of default.
43. Section 7(4) of the Code requires the Adjudicating
Authority to ascertain the existence of a default within
fourteen days of receipt of the application. That
timeline is unintelligible if "ascertainment" is read to
mean a full reconciliation of every contested ledger
entry, every interest-rate reset and every rupee of
appropriation across separate facilities spanning

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 27 of 50
several years. The fourteen day window is the period
allotted for a summary determination of a historical
fact, and the legislature in prescribing this time has
itself implicitly indicated the nature of the enquiry it
contemplates. For the purposes of Section 7,
therefore, the Adjudicating Authority is concerned
only with the existence of a financial debt and the
occurrence of default. It is not required to determine,
to the last rupee, the exact outstanding liability, as a
civil court would in a suit for recovery of money.
44. The standard applicable at the admission stage is one
of preponderance of probabilities upon the
documentary material placed on record. The
threshold is deliberately modest which is a summary,
prima facie finding of financial debt and default,
grounded in documentary evidence, rather than a full
trial upon disputed facts. It is the substance of
default, not the technical formality of proof, that must
govern proceedings under Section 7. Where the
records of an Information Utility by themselves, or the
loan documents, account statements, balance
confirmations, acknowledgements of liability, one-time settlement proposals and contemporaneous
correspondence taken collectively, demonstrate that a
sum exceeding the statutory threshold had become

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 28 of 50
due and remained unpaid, the Adjudicating Authority
is not expected to defer admission merely because the
parties dispute the computation of interest, penal
charges or other accounting entries. Such disputes
may bear upon the ultimate quantification of the
claim but they do not negate the occurrence of
default.
45. The conclusion that the Adjudicating Authority under
the Section 7 proceedings is not required to adjudicate
upon the exact quantum of debt due from a corporate
debtor is confirmed by the internal architecture of the
Code, which draws a clear line between the threshold
determination of debt and default under Section 7 and
the verification and quantification of claims during
the CIRP. Upon admission, the Interim Resolution
Professional is charged under Section 18(b) of the
Code with the receipt and collation of all claims. The
IBBI (CIRP) Regulations, 2016 empower him to call for
such evidence or clarification as he deems fit in
substantiation of a claim in whole or in part, to verify
every claim so received, and to maintain a list of
creditors recording, against each, the amount claimed
and the amount admitted. The Committee of Creditors
is then constituted under Section 21 of the Code upon
the claims so admitted.

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 29 of 50
46. The role so cast upon the Resolution Professional is
administrative and not quasi-judicial in character, his
determinations being subject throughout to the
oversight of the Adjudicating Authority. That is
precisely the point. The Code establishes a two-stage
process i.e. a summary determination of default at the
threshold, and a detailed verification of quantum
thereafter, with judicial supervision available at the
second stage. Were the Adjudicating Authority
required at admission to determine conclusively the
precise outstanding liability, the functions entrusted
to the Resolution Professional under Section 18 of the
code and IBBI(CIRP) Regulations would be rendered
otiose. A construction producing that result cannot be
correct. The trigger for initiation of the CIRP is the
occurrence of a default, not the final adjudication of
the creditor's entire claim.
47. Question I as framed in paragraph 34 above is
answered accordingly in terms that the evidentiary
threshold for satisfying the Adjudicating Authority
that a default within the meaning of Sections 3(12)
and 7 has occurred is a summary, prima facie
threshold, to be discharged upon the preponderance
of probabilities from the documentary material placed
on record. It requires a proof of the occurrence of

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 30 of 50
default, a static historical event, and not the
conclusive determination of the quantum of debt
outstanding. Disputes as to quantification do not
negate default and do not arrest admission as long as
the statutory threshold requirement under Section 4
of the Code is satisfied.
48. Since Section 7 of the Code does not contemplate a
forensic reconstruction of accounts, the Code and the
Regulations promulgated thereunder furnish
guidance upon what documentary material the
Adjudicating Authority may treat as sufficient. That
guidance yields a hierarchy.
49. Section 7(3)(a) of the Code requires the financial
creditor to furnish, with the Section 7 application,
"record of the default recorded with the information
utility or such other record or evidence of default as
may be specified". Section 7(4) of the Code provides:
"(4) The Adjudicating Authority shall, within fourteen
days of the receipt of the application under sub-section (2), ascertain the existence of a default from
the records of an information utility or on the basis of
other evidence furnished by the financial creditor
under sub-section (3)."
50. Section 7(3)(a) places the record of default with the
Information Utility first among the materials the
financial creditor may furnish, and Section 7(4)
directs ascertainment "from the records of an

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 31 of 50
information utility", and only in the alternative,
signalled by the disjunctive "or", upon the basis of
other evidence. The Information Utility record is thus,
by statutory design, a self-sufficient basis for the
Adjudicating Authority's ascertainment. It is not one
item among many in an undifferentiated evidentiary
mass.
51. The operational procedure underlying an information
utility record as provided in the IBBI (Information
Utility) regulations deserves statement, since it
explains the weight an authenticated record carries.
A creditor submitting information of default must
furnish proof of the debt and proof of the default, so
that what is placed before the Information Utility is
not a bare assertion but a documented filing
supported at the threshold by the underlying record.
The Information Utility then delivers that information
to the debtor, seeking confirmation within the
specified time, and upon his failure to respond issues
three reminders, allowing seven days in each
instance. Only two consequences follow. Where the
debtor confirms the information of default, or does not
respond even after three reminders, the status
recorded is that of authenticated and a Record of
Default is issued. Where the debtor disputes it, the

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 32 of 50
status recorded is that of disputed and what is issued
is an Information of Dispute. The mechanism is
disciplined at both ends: the creditor must
substantiate the default when he files it, and the
debtor is notified, reminded three times over, and
invited to give reasons and evidence before a Record
of Default is issued. It thus gives such records a
reliability exceeding that of ordinary private
documents, because it embeds within the record itself
the debtor's own opportunity, and failure, to
contradict it.
52. The legal weight that ought to be given to an
authenticated information utility record finds
reinforcement in the general law of evidence. The
process of authentication functions, in substance, as
an admission of the debt and the default as between
the parties to it. A debtor who does not dispute a
default recorded against it within the authentication
window has, by its conduct, permitted the creditor
and the other stakeholders in the process to treat that
default as accepted. Section 31 of the Indian Evidence
Act, 1872 (hereinafter, "IEA") or Section 25 of the
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (hereinafter,
"BSA") clarifies that such an admission is not by itself
conclusive proof of the matter admitted, but expressly

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 33 of 50
provides that an admission may operate as an
estoppel under the provisions that follow. Section 115
of the IEA or Section 121 of the BSA embodies exactly
that estoppel, precluding a party who by its
declaration, act or omission has intentionally caused
or permitted another to believe a thing to be true and
to act upon that belief from afterwards denying its
truth.
53. A corporate debtor which allows an Information Utility
record to go unchallenged through the authentication
process, thereby causing the Adjudicating Authority
and the financial creditor to proceed upon the footing
that default is undisputed, cannot subsequently be
heard to deny the fact of that default in the Section 7
proceedings itself. The "not conclusive" language of
Section 31 of the IEA and the estoppel under Section
115 of the IEA are not in conflict but they answer two
different questions. Section 31 of the IEA clarifies that
an authenticated record is not, as a matter of general
evidentiary theory incapable of being contradicted by
any evidence whatsoever. Section 115 tells us that a
particular debtor, in those circumstances, is
precluded from being the party to contradict it.
54. The evidentiary burden upon a corporate debtor
seeking to rebut a record of default issued upon

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 34 of 50
authenticated status is accordingly substantially
higher than the ordinary threshold of a mere plausible
dispute or a bare preponderance arising from self-serving assertions. To permit easy rebuttal of such
documentary evidence through bald denials would
defeat the legislative intent underlying Chapter V of
Part IV of the Code relating to information utilities
and would return the law to the very condition of
years-long factual controversy regarding the existence
of default in the first place which the BLRC identified
as the principal source of delay in insolvency
resolution proceedings.
55. It can accordingly be said that an authenticated
Information Utility record, that is to say a Record of
Default, does not become irrebuttable or legally
conclusive proof of default in the abstract, but it
creates a presumption of very high evidentiary value,
displaceable only by clear, cogent, credible and
compelling material, and not by bare denial, by
bookkeeping disagreement, or by a claim
unsupported by any material whatsoever. In the
absence of material displacing such presumption, the
Record of default, standing alone is sufficient to prima
facie establish the occurrence of default for the
purposes of Section 7.

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 35 of 50
56. Where the Information Utility record is unavailable, or
is contested upon grounds requiring more than bare
denial to resolve, or is simply not the sole plank upon
which the financial creditor has chosen to rest, the
Code and the relevant Rules supply an alternative
body of material to establish default under Section 7.
Documents as given under Part V of Form 1 appended
to the Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Application to
Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016 inter-alia include
an order of a court, tribunal or arbitral panel
adjudicating upon the default, the latest and complete
copy of the financial contract reflecting all
amendments and waivers to date, a record of default
as available with any credit information company,
copies of entries in a bankers book in accordance with
the Bankers Books Evidence Act, 1891 and it even
includes a Record of default with the information
utility, if available.
57. None of that material as enumerated in Part V of Form
1 of the IBC (Application to Adjudicatory Authority)
Rules, 2016 be treated as sufficient upon its own in
the manner that a record of default issued by an
Information Utility is, as it operates upon a different
legal footing. Taken collectively, and weighed against
one another, it may establish the occurrence of

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 36 of 50
default upon the summary standard which governs
Section 7. The governing test at this tier, in relation to
documents other than the information utility record,
is not one of strict evidentiary admissibility as
required in a civil trial. It is whether the documentary
material before the Adjudicating Authority objectively
and collectively demonstrates that a financial debt
became due and remained unpaid, so as to constitute
a 'default' warranting initiation of the CIRP.
58. Question II as framed in paragraph 34 above is thus,
answered that the documentary material upon which
the Adjudicating Authority may find its satisfaction
admits of a hierarchy. At the first tier stands a record
of default issued by an Information Utility, which is
by itself sufficient, carrying a presumption of high
evidentiary value displaceable only by clear, cogent,
credible and compelling material. At the second tier
stands the body of other documentary material
enumerated in Part V of Form 1 of IBC (Application to
Adjudicatory authority) Rules, 2016 and its
analogues, none of which is individually sufficient in
the same manner as record of default issued by an
Information Utility, but which, if taken collectively,
may establish default upon the summary standard
governing Section 7.

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 37 of 50
59. Applying that hierarchy to the case at hand, two
distinct points arise, and neither should be conflated
with the other. The first concerns the Information
Utility record. Four Form-D filings recording a default
were registered with NeSL on 09.02.2023, and those
records stood deemed authenticated as the IBBI
(Information Utilities) Regulations then provided.
Such authentication does not conclusively establish
the precise quantum in default. It does, however,
amount to a statutory acknowledgement of the
occurrence of default, carrying substantial
evidentiary value and operating as a deemed
admission of that fact. The first tier thus served its
purpose, it confirmed that a default was registered
against these facilities and went unchallenged.
60. The Appellants contend that the NeSL filings recorded
the full outstanding under each facility as being in
default before the recall notice was issued, and that a
loan not yet recalled could not be treated as wholly in
default and further, that the facility-wise figures
recorded with NeSL do not correspond to the smaller,
date-specific figures relied upon in the petition. That
contention misapprehends the function which the
Information Utility record performed in this case, and
leads to the second point.

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 38 of 50
61. The second concerns the figure of Rs.17,16,29,518/-,
upon which both forums relied as the total default as
on 15.11.2022 in respect of the Corporate Debtor, and
the corresponding minimum figure of
Rs.2,64,99,473/- in respect of Neo. Because the
Corporate Debtor's case throughout was that the
alleged default stood cured upon the proper
application of the DSRA and CMA mechanisms, and
not that no default had occurred, the enquiry below
was necessarily directed to the narrower question
whether that contention of the corporate debtor was
sustainable, and not to reconciling the facility-wise
figures recorded with the Information Utility against
the date-specific computation of default. The figure
was drawn cumulatively from the Statement of
Accounts, furnished by the Financial Creditor, never
disputed as to authenticity and produced by the
Corporate Debtor itself, from other documents such
as the two BK Ramadhyani review reports, which
questioned only the rate of interest and not the
computation of default, from the recall notice and
from the Corporate Debtor's own letters of 23.12.2022
and 11.01.2023 seeking a settlement upon the footing
of an admitted shortfall. This is the second tier
operating exactly as designed. Where the fact of
default is not genuinely disputed, the role of the first

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 39 of 50
tier was to confirm that a default was registered and
went unchallenged, while the quantum crossing the
statutory threshold was properly drawn from the
fuller, collective record. There is no inconsistency
between the two, and no error of law appears in the
approach adopted by the tribunals below.
62. Both figures in the Section 7 petition comfortably
exceed the minimum threshold prescribed under
Section 4. The precise reconciliation of the aggregate
against the figures which each NeSL Form-D
separately records is accordingly immaterial to the
outcome. That follows directly from the static-default
principle established in answer to Question I framed
by this court. Once a default of a magnitude
comfortably crossing the threshold is shown by
material that is not genuinely disputed, the Corporate
Debtor's contentions upon the CMA and the DSRA
having been addressed upon a consideration of the
relevant provisions of each by both the Adjudicating
Authority and the Appellate Tribunal, further
precision in quantification is a matter for the claims
process during the CIRP, and not a precondition to
admission under Section 7.
63. The letter dated 23.12.2022, written by appellant no.1
on behalf of the Corporate Debtor and Neo to its

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 40 of 50
lenders within six weeks of the pleaded date of default
and before the assignment, is to the same effect. It
recorded that the escalation in the rate of interest by
the lender had severely curtailed plans to commence
repayment of principal and that the entire surplus
cash flow had been absorbed in servicing the
additional interest. That the revenues had fallen by
more than ninety per cent during the pandemic, some
four hundred employees had been retrenched and the
hotel at Pune had remained closed from May 2021 to
January 2022, the companies had at times been
unable to meet salaries or the cost of maintaining the
hotel and that the ECLGS facilities had been applied
principally towards payment of the lenders' interest
and repayment of the loan. The letter is a
contemporaneous document of the companies' own
authorship, written before the institution of these
proceedings and untouched by the exigencies of
litigation, its contents cannot be reconciled with the
case now advanced that nothing stood due and
unpaid as on 15.11.2022. To this must be added the
admission recorded by the High Court of Karnataka
in the proceedings instituted by the Corporate Debtor
itself, regarding certain overdue principal and
interest. An admission recorded in judicial proceeding
instituted by the party making it is binding upon that

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 41 of 50
party and cannot be resiled from in collateral
proceedings.
64. There is finally a finding at paragraph 6.6 of the order
of the Adjudicating Authority which is of particular
significance. The adjudicating authority found that
the cash accruals available with the Corporate Debtor
remained insufficient, right up to December 2023, to
meet its service obligations under the credit facilities,
and that a default persisted through that subsequent
period as well, even leaving aside the recall of the
whole of the facilities. That independently undercuts
the assertion that the default as on 15.11.2022 was
capable of being cured. The shortfall was not a
momentary occurrence, attributable ostensibly to a
mis-appropriation of the Retention Account in a single
month, it continued month upon month, up to the
very eve of the first admission order of the
Adjudicating Authority.
65. The contention of the Appellants that the Corporate
Debtor and Neo are profitable businesses and their
admission into CIRP is contrary to the object of the
Code, requires a considered answer, both as a matter
of law and as a matter of the economic premise upon
which it rests. Viewed from an economic perspective,
it conflates two distinct concepts. A profitable

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 42 of 50
company with a positive EBITDA may nonetheless be
wholly unable to service its debt if the repayment
obligations falling due exceed its operating profit.
Conversely, a loss-making company may have ample
liquidity to meet its obligations. EBITDA, being
earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and
amortisation, is by definition computed before
interest, and says nothing whatsoever about a
company's capacity to meet cash obligations to its
lenders as and when they fall due. The metric relevant
to that question is the Debt Service Coverage Ratio.
The Corporate Debtor's own audited financial
statements record a Debt Service Coverage Ratio of
0.12 for the financial year 2022-23, meaning that its
internal accruals covered only 12 per cent of that
year's debt obligations. It is a figure the Appellants
cannot dispute as it was drawn from their own books.
Profitability is accordingly not merely legally irrelevant
to the existence of default under Section 7 but an
economically unreliable proxy for solvency.
66. It is appropriate to state the underlying principle,
since the debate regarding profitability and solvency
recurs in matters of this kind. The Code is premised
upon timely intervention rather than terminal
insolvency. Its objective is not to defer insolvency

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 43 of 50
proceedings until the corporate debtor has
deteriorated to a stage at which liquidation is the only
remaining outcome, but to identify and resolve
financial stress at its earliest legally cognisable
manifestation, namely the occurrence of a default. It
is for this reason that the legislature has adopted
"default" under Section 3(12), and not commercial or
balance-sheet insolvency as the jurisdictional trigger.
Any interpretation requiring a financial creditor to
await the corporate debtor's irreversible financial
collapse before invoking the Code would undermine
its preventive and remedial architecture and defeat its
central objective of facilitating resolution in preference
to liquidation.
67. The conclusions reached by this Court upon both the
questions of law find further reinforcement in the
amendments effected to Section 7(5) of the Code by
the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (Amendment)
Act, 2026, notified in April 2026. Section 7(5), as
amended, provides:
"(5) The Adjudicating Authority shall, within
fourteen days of the receipt of the application under
sub-section (2), by an order-
(a) admit the application, if it is satisfied that a
default has occurred and the application under sub-section (2) is complete, and there is no disciplinary
proceeding pending against the proposed resolution
professional; or
xxx xxx xxx

Explanation I.-For the purposes of this sub-section, it is hereby clarified that where the
requirements under clause (a) have been complied
with, no other ground shall be considered to reject an

Explanation II.-For the removal of doubts, it is
hereby clarified that where a record of default in

been furnished along with the application filed by

68. The amendment operates upon this field in three
respects. First, the substitution of "shall" for "may" in
Section 7(5)(a) leaves no room for a discretion to
refuse admission once the statutory conditions are
satisfied, the Adjudicating Authority being now
mandated, and no longer merely permitted, to admit
a Section 7 application. Secondly, Explanation I
provides that upon satisfaction of those conditions in
Section 7(5)(a), no other ground shall be considered
for rejection, thereby confining the Adjudicating
Authority to an examination of whether the statutory
preconditions exist and excluding every consideration
dehors the statute. Thirdly, Explanation II declares a
Record of Default accompanying the application
"sufficient" for ascertainment, the use of that word
with "shall" signifying that the creditor's evidentiary
burden to prove a default stands discharged upon its

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 45 of 50
production and that no independent or additional
evidence may be insisted upon by the Adjudicating
Authority.
69. Neither explanation creates new law. Both are
introduced by the familiar language of clarification
and removal of doubt, and neither alters the pre-existing position, each makes explicit only what was
already implicit in the Code. The sufficiency of an
Information Utility record was already carried by
Section 7(4) and by the design of the Code. The
hierarchy set out in answer to the second question of
law framed in paragraph 34 above is thus placed
beyond cavil by express legislative enactment, and the
reasoning of this Court would have been identical had
the amendment not been effectuated.
70. A word is due upon the Information Utility mechanism
itself. It is an innovation of Indian origin, without any
direct parallel in comparable insolvency regimes at
the time of its introduction. A regulated repository of
financial information, authenticated through the
debtor's own participation or acquiescence, designed
so that the fact of default may be ascertained at the
threshold without recourse to a protracted enquiry.
Almost ten years have now passed since the Code
came into force. The framework has matured,

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 46 of 50
financial creditors submit the information of default
as a matter of routine, and the corporate debtors can
no longer claim unfamiliarity either with the process
of authentication or with the consequences of silence.
The Bankruptcy Law Reforms Committee's
observation that until Information Utilities became
ubiquitous financial creditors might establish default
in the manner available to operational creditors was
addressed to a period of transition and that period has
long passed. It is accordingly imperative that the
Adjudicating Authorities accord the weight which the
Code, and now Explanation II to the amended Section
7(5), assign to it.
71. It is convenient to summarise the conclusions
reached:
(i) The jurisdiction of this Court under Section 62 of
the Code is confined to questions of law arising out of
the order of the Appellate Tribunal. Where the
Adjudicating Authority and the Appellate Tribunal
have concurrently returned findings of fact and law
upon the same material, those findings are not to be
disturbed unless shown to be perverse, based upon
no evidence, arrived at by ignoring material evidence,
or founded upon an erroneous legal standard.

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 47 of 50
(ii) The status of the Respondent no.1 as a financial
creditor within the meaning of Section 5(7) of the Code
stands conclusively established by the Assignment
Agreement dated 27.12.2022, the validity of which
has been upheld by the High Court of Karnataka and
affirmed by this Court. The challenge to the
assignment is barred by the principles of issue
estoppel.
(iii) Section 7 of the Code establishes a summary
jurisdiction. The evidentiary threshold for
ascertaining default is that of preponderance of
probabilities upon the documentary material placed
on record, and not a forensic reconciliation of
accounts. The occurrence of a default is a static
historical event whereas the quantum of a debt
outstanding is dynamic. The role of the Adjudicating
Authority at the admission stage is confined to
ascertaining the existence of debt and default.
(iv) The documentary evidence upon which the
Adjudicating Authority may record its satisfaction
admits of a hierarchy. At the first tier stands a record
of default issued by an Information Utility, which is
by itself sufficient and which creates a presumption
of high evidentiary value, displaceable only by clear,
cogent, credible and compelling material and not by

C.A. No. 12195/2025 Page 48 of 50
bare denial or bookkeeping disagreement. At the
second tier stands the other documentary material
enumerated in Part V of Form 1 of the Insolvency and
Bankruptcy (Application to Adjudicating Authority)
Rules, 2016 and its analogues which inter-alia
includes loan agreements, statements of account,
balance confirmations, acknowledgements of liability,
and contemporaneous correspondence, which, taken
collectively, may establish default upon the summary
standard governing Section 7.
(v) Profitability is neither legally relevant to, nor
economically probative of, the capacity to service debt.
The Code proceeds upon the principle of timely
intervention rather than terminal insolvency, and
adopts 'default' under Section 3(12) of the Code, not
commercial or balance-sheet insolvency, as the
jurisdictional trigger.
(vi) Upon the record in these appeals, a default above
the threshold prescribed under Section 4 of the Code
is established.
